options.B: References to the repealed provision must be read literally as referring only to the original 1956 Act forever, regardless of any later repeal and re-enactment

question_html: Under section 9 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, what is the effect of using the words 'from' and 'to' in describing a series of days or period of time in any legislation or regulation?

options.A: It is sufficient, for the purpose of excluding the first day in a series of days or period of time, to use the word 'from'; and, for the purpose of including the last day in that series or period, to use the word 'to' - so a period described as running 'from' a given date excludes that date, while a period running 'to' a given date includes that date
options.B: The words 'from' and 'to' are legally interchangeable and produce identical results under section 9, with no difference in whether the stated date is included or excluded
options.C: Section 9 provides that both the first and the last day of any stated period are always excluded, regardless of whether 'from' or 'to' is used
options.D: Section 9 provides that both the first and the last day of any stated period are always included, regardless of whether 'from' or 'to' is used

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) It is sufficient, for the purpose of excluding the first day in a series of days or period of time, to use the word 'from'; and, for the purpose of including the last day in that series or period, to use the word 'to' - so a period described as running 'from' a given date excludes that date, while a period running 'to' a given date includes that date

options.D: The act or proceeding must instead be done on the day immediately BEFORE the last day of the prescribed period, working backwards from the closure

question_html: What do clauses (1) and (2) of section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 respectively provide regarding gender and number, and what caution does the study material note about applying section 13(1) to matters of succession?

options.A: Section 13(1) provides that masculine words include females only in criminal statutes, and section 13(2) provides that singular words never include the plural under any circumstances
options.B: Section 13 applies without any exception or limitation whatsoever, including in succession law, so 'male descendants' has always been judicially interpreted to include female descendants

answer_html:

question_html: Under section 14 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, once a Central Act or Regulation confers a power, how often may that power be exercised, unless a different intention appears; and under section 15, where a power to appoint a person to an office is conferred, how may such an appointment be made, unless otherwise expressly provided?

options.A: Under section 14, the power may be exercised from time to time as occasion requires, unless a different intention appears - as applied by the Supreme Court to the Chief Justice's power under section 51(3) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; under section 15, any such appointment may be made either by name or by virtue of office (ex-officio), unless otherwise expressly provided
options.B: Under section 14, a conferred power may be exercised only once and is thereafter permanently exhausted, and under section 15, an appointment can only ever be made by name and never by virtue of an office
options.C: Under section 14, a conferred power lapses automatically after 90 days if not exercised, and under section 15, ex-officio appointments are prohibited under the General Clauses Act
options.D: Section 14 applies only to judicial powers and section 15 applies only to legislative powers, with neither section applying to executive or administrative appointments

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Under section 14, the power may be exercised from time to time as occasion requires, unless a different intention appears - as applied by the Supreme Court to the Chief Justice's power under section 51(3) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; under section 15, any such appointment may be made either by name or by virtue of office (ex-officio), unless otherwise expressly provided

Section 14 permits a conferred power to be exercised repeatedly, from time to time as occasion requires, while section 15 permits an appointment power to be exercised either by naming a specific individual or ex-officio (by virtue of holding a specified office), unless the enactment otherwise expressly provides.

question_html: Under section 16 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, what additional power does the authority having the power to appoint also possess; and under section 18, for what purpose is it sufficient for a Central Act or Regulation to merely express its relation to a functionary or corporation, rather than naming every individual successor?

options.A: Under section 16, the appointing authority has no power at all to suspend or dismiss any appointee, and such power must always be separately and expressly granted; under section 18, every successor must be individually named in the Act for the law to apply to them
options.B: Under section 16, the authority having power to make an appointment for the time being also has the power to suspend or dismiss any person so appointed, whether appointed by itself or by any other authority in exercise of that power - illustrated by the power to appoint a receiver under Order 40, Rule 1(a) of the CPC, 1908, being construed to include the power to remove the receiver; under section 18, it is sufficient to express a law's relation to the functionaries or corporations themselves, and this is deemed to indicate its relation to their successors as well (for functionaries) or to corporations having perpetual succession
options.C: Section 16 applies only to judicial appointments and section 18 applies only to corporate mergers, with neither section having any bearing on administrative appointments or ordinary succession
options.D: Under section 16, only a superior authority (never the original appointing authority) may suspend or dismiss an appointee, and under section 18, successors are never covered unless a fresh Act is separately passed for each successor

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Under section 16, the authority having power to make an appointment for the time being also has the power to suspend or dismiss any person so appointed, whether appointed by itself or by any other authority in exercise of that power - illustrated by the power to appoint a receiver under Order 40, Rule 1(a) of the CPC, 1908, being construed to include the power to remove the receiver; under section 18, it is sufficient to express a law's relation to the functionaries or corporations themselves, and this is deemed to indicate its relation to their successors as well (for functionaries) or to corporations having perpetual succession

Section 16 vests the power to suspend or dismiss in whichever authority currently holds the power to appoint (whoever originally made the appointment), while section 18 dispenses with the need to separately name successors - a law's expressed relation to a functionary or corporation is read as extending automatically to that functionary's or corporation's successors.

question_html: Under section 17 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, is it necessary to name a specific individual officeholder for a law to apply to whoever currently executes that office's functions; and under section 19, does a law relating to the chief or superior of an office extend to a deputy or subordinate lawfully performing that superior's duties?

options.A: Under section 17, a law applies only if it names the individual officeholder by their personal name, and under section 19, a law relating to a superior officer never extends to any deputy or subordinate under any circumstances
options.B: Section 17 applies only to judicial officers and section 19 applies only to elected legislators, with neither provision extending to administrative or executive officeholders
options.C: Under section 17, it is sufficient to mention the official title of the officer presently executing the functions (or the officer by whom the functions are commonly executed), without needing to name the specific individual, for the law to apply to whoever holds that office from time to time; under section 19, yes - a law relative to the chief or superior of an office shall apply to the deputies or subordinates lawfully performing the duties of that office in the superior's place, so as to prescribe the superior's own duty
options.D: Under section 17, the law lapses entirely whenever the named officeholder retires or is replaced, and under section 19, deputies and subordinates are always excluded from the scope of laws relating to their superior

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Under section 17, it is sufficient to mention the official title of the officer presently executing the functions (or the officer by whom the functions are commonly executed), without needing to name the specific individual, for the law to apply to whoever holds that office from time to time; under section 19, yes - a law relative to the chief or superior of an office shall apply to the deputies or subordinates lawfully performing the duties of that office in the superior's place, so as to prescribe the superior's own duty

Section 17 allows a law to apply by reference to an official title rather than a named individual, so it automatically applies to whoever currently or commonly executes that office's functions, while section 19 extends a law relating to a superior officer to a deputy or subordinate lawfully performing that superior's duties in their place.

question_html: Under section 20 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, what meaning do expressions used in a notification, order, scheme, rule, form, or bye-law carry, unless repugnant to the subject or context; and under section 21, does the power to issue such an instrument also include the power to add to, amend, vary, or rescind it?

options.A: Under section 20, expressions in subordinate instruments always carry their ordinary dictionary meaning regardless of the parent Act, and under section 21, a power to issue an instrument is exhausted the moment it is first exercised and can never be used again to amend it
options.B: Section 20 applies only to Ordinances and section 21 applies only to Constitutional Amendments, with neither provision governing rules, orders, or bye-laws issued under an ordinary Central Act
options.C: Under section 20, expressions in subordinate instruments must always be re-defined afresh within that very instrument, and under section 21, only the original issuing authority (and no successor authority) may ever amend or rescind the instrument
options.D: Under section 20, such expressions carry the same respective meaning as in the Act or Regulation conferring the power to issue them, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context - illustrated by the term 'collector' in Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 bearing the same meaning as in section 3(c) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; under section 21, yes - a power to issue a notification, order, rule, or bye-law includes, in like manner and subject to like sanction and conditions, the power to add to, amend, vary, or rescind it, and (per Shreesidhbali Steels Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh) this power can be exercised from time to time, not merely once

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Under section 20, such expressions carry the same respective meaning as in the Act or Regulation conferring the power to issue them, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context - illustrated by the term 'collector' in Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 bearing the same meaning as in section 3(c) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; under section 21, yes - a power to issue a notification, order, rule, or bye-law includes, in like manner and subject to like sanction and conditions, the power to add to, amend, vary, or rescind it, and (per Shreesidhbali Steels Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh) this power can be exercised from time to time, not merely once

Section 20 ties the meaning of expressions in a notification/order/rule/bye-law to the parent Act or Regulation conferring the power, and section 21 extends the power to issue such an instrument to also cover adding to, amending, varying, or rescinding it - a power that, per Shreesidhbali Steels Ltd., may be exercised repeatedly over time, not just once.

question_html: Under section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, where an act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments, may the offender be prosecuted and punished under more than one of them, and what single restriction does the section impose?

options.A: The offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall NOT be punished twice for the same offence - the Supreme Court has clarified that section 26 bars only double punishment, not trial or conviction under two enactments, and this restriction (mirrored in Article 20(2) of the Constitution) applies only when the two offences being prosecuted are truly the same, i.e., their ingredients are identical
options.B: The offender can only be prosecuted and punished under whichever enactment was passed first in time, and prosecution under any later enactment is automatically barred
options.C: The offender can never be prosecuted or tried under more than one enactment at all, even where the two offences have entirely distinct ingredients
options.D: The offender must always be punished under BOTH enactments simultaneously and cumulatively, with no bar on double punishment for the same offence

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall NOT be punished twice for the same offence - the Supreme Court has clarified that section 26 bars only double punishment, not trial or conviction under two enactments, and this restriction (mirrored in Article 20(2) of the Constitution) applies only when the two offences being prosecuted are truly the same, i.e., their ingredients are identical

Section 26 permits prosecution and punishment under either or any of the enactments creating the offence, but prohibits punishing the offender twice for the same offence - as clarified in State of M.P. v. V.R. Agnihotri, an acquittal on one alternative charge does not bar conviction on the other, and the double-punishment bar applies only where the two offences share identical ingredients.

question_html: Under section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, where any legislation or regulation requires a document to be served by post, how (unless a different intention appears) shall such service be deemed to be effected, and when is the letter deemed delivered?

options.A: Service by post is deemed effected merely by handing the letter, unaddressed and unstamped, to any private courier company, with no requirement of registered post at all
options.B: Service by post is deemed effected by (i) properly addressing, (ii) pre-paying, and (iii) posting the letter containing the document by registered post; the letter is deemed to have been effected (delivered) at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post
options.C: Service by post requires the document to be sent by speed post only, and registered post is expressly excluded as a valid mode of deemed service under section 27
options.D: Section 27 deems service effected only upon the recipient's personal written acknowledgment of receipt, regardless of whether the letter was properly addressed, pre-paid, or posted by registered post

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Service by post is deemed effected by (i) properly addressing, (ii) pre-paying, and (iii) posting the letter containing the document by registered post; the letter is deemed to have been effected (delivered) at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post

Section 27 deems postal service effected upon proper addressing, pre-payment, and posting by registered post, with delivery deemed to occur when the letter would ordinarily be delivered in the course of post - as illustrated in Jagdish Singh v. Applying section 9 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, within which dates must Meridian Foods Ltd. pay the dividend declared at its AGM held on 20th September, 2024?

options.A: The window is from 20th September, 2024 to 19th October, 2024 (both days inclusive), since the declaration date itself must always be included and the 30th day excluded
options.B: The window is a fixed calendar month, i.e., the whole of October 2024, since 'within 30 days' under the Companies Act, 2013 is deemed equivalent to 'within one calendar month'
options.C: Applying section 9, the 30-day period runs 'from' 20th September, 2024, so that date is excluded, and the period runs 'to' the 30th day, which is included - the 30-day window is therefore from 21st September, 2024 to 20th October, 2024 (both days inclusive)
options.D: The window is from 20th September, 2024 to 20th November, 2024 (both days inclusive), treating the 30-day period as 30 weeks rather than 30 days

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Applying section 9, the 30-day period runs 'from' 20th September, 2024, so that date is excluded, and the period runs 'to' the 30th day, which is included - the 30-day window is therefore from 21st September, 2024 to 20th October, 2024 (both days inclusive)

Under section 9 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, 'from' excludes the first day (20th September, 2024) and 'to' includes the last day, so the 30-day dividend payment window runs from 21st September, 2024 to 20th October, 2024, both days inclusive.

options.A: Section 9 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides that it is sufficient, for the purpose of excluding the first day in a series of days or period of time, to use the word 'from', and for the purpose of including the last day in that series or period, to use the word 'to' - this single 'commencement and termination of time' rule governs the computation of both statutory windows

Correct answer: (A) Section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which provides that words in the singular shall include the plural (and vice versa) unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context - this provision is directly relevant to reading the singular phrase 'its subsidiary company' in section 203(3) of the Companies Act, 2013

Section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 is the operative provision here - it extends singular expressions to include the plural unless repugnant to the subject or context, which is precisely the interpretive question raised by section 203(3)'s use of the singular 'its subsidiary company'.

Applying section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, does the repeal of the Waterford Textile Mills (Nationalisation) Act, by itself, extinguish the rights, liabilities and pending proceedings that had already accrued against or in favour of Fairmont Spinning Ltd. under that Act before its repeal?

options.B: Yes - under section 6, only pending litigation is preserved after a repeal, while all previously accrued rights, privileges, and liabilities are automatically wiped out

question_html:
Mr. Devendra, a director of Vantage Engineering Ltd., took an action in the course of his duties that, on the given facts, constitutes an offence both under a provision of the Companies Act, 2013 and, separately, under a corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Mr. Devendra maintains that his action, though it turned out to be based on a mistaken factual belief, was nonetheless taken honestly and in good faith - although he candidly admits that he did not exercise particular due care or make further enquiries before acting.

Since Mr. Devendra's act constitutes an offence under both the Companies Act, 2013 and the Indian Penal Code, 1860, applying section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, may he be prosecuted under both enactments, and may he be punished under both for the same offence?

options.A: Mr. Devendra can be prosecuted under only whichever enactment carries the more severe penalty, with the other enactment becoming entirely inapplicable to him under section 26
options.B: Mr. Devendra may be prosecuted and, if the ingredients are made out, punished under either or any of the two enactments, but he shall not be punished twice for the same offence - section 26 bars only double punishment, not trial or conviction under both enactments, as the Supreme Court has clarified that there is no bar to trial or conviction under two enactments, only to punishing the offender twice for the same offence
options.C: Mr. Devendra must necessarily be punished cumulatively and simultaneously under BOTH enactments in full, since section 26 mandates double punishment wherever an act violates two enactments
options.D: Mr. Devendra cannot be prosecuted at all under either enactment, since section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 operates as a complete bar on prosecution wherever an act constitutes an offence under more than one law

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Mr. Devendra may be prosecuted and, if the ingredients are made out, punished under either or any of the two enactments, but he shall not be punished twice for the same offence - section 26 bars only double punishment, not trial or conviction under both enactments, as the Supreme Court has clarified that there is no bar to trial or conviction under two enactments, only to punishing the offender twice for the same offence

Section 26 permits prosecution and punishment under either or any of the enactments creating the offence, while barring only a second punishment for the same offence - trial or conviction under both enactments is not itself prohibited, only double punishment is.

question_html:
Mr. Devendra, a director of Vantage Engineering Ltd., took an action in the course of his duties that, on the given facts, constitutes an offence both under a provision of the Companies Act, 2013 and, separately, under a corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Mr. Devendra maintains that his action, though it turned out to be based on a mistaken factual belief, was nonetheless taken honestly and in good faith - although he candidly admits that he did not exercise particular due care or make further enquiries before acting.

Suppose, on closer examination, the ingredients constituting the offence under the Companies Act, 2013 provision are found to be materially different from the ingredients constituting the offence under the Indian Penal Code, 1860 provision relied upon against Mr. Devendra. Would the section 26 bar against double punishment, and the corresponding protection under Article 20(2) of the Constitution, apply in that situation?

options.A: Yes - the section 26 bar and Article 20(2) protection apply automatically whenever two enactments are invoked against the same person, irrespective of whether the ingredients of the two offences are identical or entirely different
options.B: No - section 26 has no double-punishment bar of any kind, and Article 20(2) of the Constitution deals exclusively with the right against self-incrimination rather than double punishment
options.C: No - the bar under section 26 (and the analogous protection under Article 20(2) of the Constitution against being punished twice for the 'same offence') applies only where the two offences forming the subject of prosecution are truly the same, i.e., where the ingredients constituting the two offences are identical; if the offences under the two enactments are distinct and not identical, the double-punishment bar does not apply, and Mr. Devendra could in principle be punished separately under each
options.D: It cannot be determined without first establishing whether Mr. Devendra is a first-time offender, a factor that section 26 treats as decisive regardless of whether the ingredients of the two offences are identical

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - the bar under section 26 (and the analogous protection under Article 20(2) of the Constitution against being punished twice for the 'same offence') applies only where the two offences forming the subject of prosecution are truly the same, i.e., where the ingredients constituting the two offences are identical; if the offences under the two enactments are distinct and not identical, the double-punishment bar does not apply, and Mr. Devendra could in principle be punished separately under each

The section 26 bar (and Article 20(2)) applies only when the two offences are truly the same in their ingredients - where the offences under the two enactments are distinct, with different ingredients, the double-punishment protection does not apply and separate punishment under each enactment remains possible.

Mr. Devendra admits he did not exercise due care or make further enquiries before acting, but insists his action was nonetheless honest. Applying section 3(22) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (as opposed to the different, due-care-based standard applied under some other enactments, such as the Indian Contract Act, 1872), does his admitted lack of due care, by itself, defeat his claim that the action was done in 'good faith'?

options.B: Yes - section 3(22) defines 'good faith' solely by reference to whether the actor obtained prior legal advice, making due care and honesty both legally irrelevant to the analysis
options.C: It cannot be determined, because section 3(22) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 was omitted from the Act with effect from 1st April, 2022 and no longer has any legal effect
